entities.name: Ka'aper
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ka'aper, often referred to by his modern nickname 'Sheikh el-Beled' ('Mayor of the Village'), was a prominent ancient Egyptian scribe and priest whose life bridged the late Fourth and early Fifth Dynasties, approximately around 2560 BCE. Serving during a period of profound artistic and administrative consolidation in the Old Kingdom, Ka'aper's enduring significance stems not from his political power, which was mid-level, but from the exceptionally lifelike wooden statue discovered in his mastaba tomb at Saqqara. This masterpiece of Old Kingdom sculpture provides invaluable insights into the aesthetic ideals and craftsmanship of the era, offering a rare, intimate glimpse into the visage of an elite official.

As a 'Chief Lector Priest' (Kheri-heb) and 'Scribe of the Army', Ka'aper held important administrative and religious roles within the Memphite court, overseeing rituals and maintaining records for military logistics or personnel. His tomb, Mastaba C8 (often designated 'Mastaba of Sheikh el-Beled'), situated north of the Step Pyramid of Djoser, contained a collection of artifacts, but it was the 112 cm tall sycamore fig wood statue, now a centerpiece of the Egyptian Museum in Cairo, that immortalized him. The statue, depicting a corpulent, striding man holding a staff, is remarkable for its inlaid crystal eyes, which convey an astonishing sense of vitality and individuality, transcending the more formalized representations typical of royal portraiture.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ka'aper's iconic wooden statue revolutionized the understanding of Old Kingdom non-royal portraiture, providing critical insights into the artistic sophistication and social hierarchy of ancient Egypt. It remains a celebrated artifact, shaping public perception and scholarly analysis of the era's craftsmanship.
